network: The Grand Trunk Road's precolonial corridor
title: A trunk corridor rebuilt by five empires, never the same road twice
register: documentary, and the alignment kept moving
summary: A caravan crossing the Indo-Gangetic plain used whichever stretch of road, riverbank, or ferry a given ruler happened to be maintaining that century, not one engineered highway surviving intact from the Mauryas to the Mughals. A measured royal road from the Indus to Pataliputra entered Greek geography under Chandragupta; Sher Shah Suri's sarais and relay horses and Akbar's news writers rebuilt the corridor twice more; it never closed in a single year, it just kept changing patrons, and the English name belongs to a nineteenth-century colonial reconstruction of a much older, much less continuous thing.

nodes.name: Balkh
nodes.note: Western gateway joining South Asian routes to Iranian and Central Asian systems: a source and transit region for horses, bullion, textiles and Buddhist travelers. Its treatment as a formal terminus of one ancient Indian road is a modern reconstruction, not a documented charter.

nodes.name: Kabul
nodes.note: Junction for routes through the Hindu Kush and toward Gandhara, exposed to mountain weather, narrow passes, political fragmentation and the cost of fodder and pack transport.

nodes.name: Peshawar
nodes.note: Purushapura and neighboring Pushkalavati were Gandharan urban and political centers controlling the approaches to the Khyber and Kabul valleys, linking South Asian exchange with Central Asia.

nodes.name: Taxila
nodes.note: The best-attested northwestern hinge between routes from Bactria, Kashmir, the Indus, Punjab and the Ganges plain, important from at least the first millennium BCE and successively held by Achaemenid, Macedonian, Mauryan, Indo-Greek, Saka, Parthian and Kushan regimes before its early-medieval decline.

nodes.name: Rohtas
nodes.note: Begun by Sher Shah after defeating Humayun, principally to command the Gakhar country. Named as the western endpoint of his road program by the chronicler Sarwani, though popular tradition sometimes stretches his road all the way to Kabul, which Rohtas is not.

nodes.name: Lahore
nodes.note: Mughal provincial capital, manufacturing and commercial center, mint, and departure point for Kashmir, Multan, Kabul, and the Delhi–Agra routes. Jahangir's memoir records its bazaars supplied with Central Asian fruit.

nodes.name: Sirhind
nodes.note: A major strategic and commercial station between Punjab and Delhi, with provincial administration, markets, gardens, religious institutions and sarais.

nodes.name: Panipat
nodes.note: An open plain that repeatedly became a battlefield, in 1526 and 1556 within this network's bound period, because armies moving between the northwest and Delhi converged on the same corridor that carried merchants and post.

nodes.name: Delhi
nodes.note: Became the decisive political and administrative hub under the Delhi Sultanate and Mughals, hosting successive cities from Qila Rai Pithora to Shahjahanabad, functioning as court, chancery, intelligence clearinghouse, mint and army-assembly point.

nodes.name: Mathura
nodes.note: Ancient religious and commercial center on the Yamuna linking the northern corridor to western and central India, drawing Buddhist, Jain and Vaishnava pilgrimage; under the Mughals it sat on the Delhi–Agra route.

nodes.name: Agra
nodes.note: Imperial capital under Akbar and Jahangir and the pivot of roads toward Delhi, Lahore, Allahabad, Ajmer, Malwa and the Deccan; the network here was never simply one northern line.

nodes.name: Kannauj
nodes.note: A major early-medieval political and commercial center, visited by Xuanzang during Harsha's reign; its prominence redirected regional traffic even where it did not sit on every reconstructed ancient alignment.

nodes.name: Prayaga-Allahabad
nodes.note: Confluence of the Ganges and Yamuna: pilgrimage center, ferry and boat-transfer node, and after Akbar's fort a major Mughal administrative and strategic station.

nodes.name: Varanasi
nodes.note: Major river port, manufacturing center, pilgrimage destination and scholarly hub, where textiles, ritual goods, money, pilgrims, mendicants, manuscripts and information converged.

nodes.name: Chunar
nodes.note: Fortified Ganges chokepoint controlling river and road movement east of Varanasi, prominent in the struggles between Sher Shah and the Mughals.

nodes.name: Sasaram
nodes.note: Sher Shah's home base and mausoleum site, symbolically anchoring Sur power in the Bihar section of the corridor.

nodes.name: Pataliputra-Patna
nodes.note: Mauryan capital and the eastern terminus of the measured royal road explicitly known to Greek geographical tradition; later Patna remained a major commercial and administrative river center.

nodes.name: Teliagarhi-Rajmahal
nodes.note: The narrow corridor between the Rajmahal Hills and the Ganges system formed the effective land gateway between Bihar and Bengal, and the customs point where goods entering from Bengal were assessed under Sher Shah's fiscal reform.

nodes.name: Gaur-Pandua
nodes.note: Successive Bengal capitals and major political, minting, commercial and religious nodes; changing river courses and disease environments altered their road importance over time.

nodes.name: Sonargaon
nodes.note: Commercial and administrative center connected to Bengal's textile-producing districts and river system; named by Sarwani as the eastern endpoint of Sher Shah's great road. It is not Chittagong, despite the popular "Kabul to Chittagong" formula.

nodes.name: Tamralipti
nodes.note: Ancient port traditionally presented as the far eastern terminus of Uttarapatha. Archaeology and literary evidence confirm it as an important eastern maritime node, but a single continuously engineered road from Taxila to here is a modern synthesis, not a documented ancient institution.

nodes.name: Chandragupta Maurya
nodes.note: Unified much of the corridor under one state and established Pataliputra as an imperial capital extending into the northwest after the settlement with Seleucus I. Whether he built the road or reorganized existing routes is disputed; no surviving edict credits him with a single continuous highway to Bengal.

nodes.name: Ashoka
nodes.note: Ordered road-related welfare works recorded in Major Rock Edict II and Major Pillar Edict VII: wells, banyan and mango trees, and watering places at intervals given in one translation as eight krosas, not the popularly repeated half-kos. The edicts speak of roads generally, not of one continuous alignment.

nodes.name: Sher Shah Suri
nodes.note: Repaired and reorganized principal roads, endowed sarais, placed postal horses, concentrated customs collection, imposed collective local responsibility for road crime, and issued the standardized silver rupiya. Died at the siege of Kalinjar in 1545, before the program's long-term consequences could be tested under his own rule.

nodes.name: Akbar
nodes.note: Absorbed Sur road, sarai and customs institutions into a larger and more durable imperial system linked to news writers, spies, provincial commands, standardized currency and measures, and military movement.

nodes.name: Jahangir
nodes.note: Issued the best-documented order for milestone construction, in 1619, under Baqir Khan's authority. The clearer textual record for Jahangir's kos minars complicates the popular claim that Sher Shah built every surviving marker.

nodes.name: Ibn Battuta
nodes.note: Traveler in India under Muhammad bin Tughluq who described the mounted ulaq and foot dawa relay posts, a runner carrying a bell-fitted rod that signaled the next station before he arrived. His comparison of five days for news against fifty for an ordinary traveler documents relay speed, not a universal timetable.

nodes.name: The Delhi Sultanate barid
nodes.note: The combined post, surveillance and reporting system: news writers, spies, provincial officers, mounted couriers and foot runners forming overlapping chains that brought distant provinces under rapid central intelligence.

nodes.name: The Mauryan royal road register
nodes.note: The measured stage list from the Indus side of India to Palibothra/Pataliputra known to Greek geography through Megasthenes and transmitted by Strabo: a road of 10,000 stadia. The exact stadium and itinerary are uncertain, so any conversion to modern distance is approximate.

nodes.name: The Tarikh-i Sher Shahi
nodes.note: Abbas Khan Sarwani's chronicle, composed under Akbar about a generation after Sher Shah's death, using Afghan informants and family connections but written under Mughal patronage. It attributes 1,700 sarais to Sher Shah, a famous but uncorroborated figure that cannot mean 1,700 structures on one road at two-kos spacing.

nodes.name: Sher Shah's rupiya coinage
nodes.note: The standardized silver rupiya, facilitating exchange across Sher Shah's dominions and surviving as the Mughal monetary standard long after his death.
